n: A new threat arises — not from outside enemies but from within. Poor families, wives included, cry out against fellow Jews who are taking advantage of them.

f.g: Fellow Israelites — making the injustice a betrayal of covenant brotherhood.

n: Large families cannot get enough grain to survive. Working on the wall may have left them less time to farm.

f.g: In KJV English, grain in general — wheat or barley, not American maize.

n: Others have mortgaged their fields, vineyards, and homes just to buy food during a famine.

f.g: Famine, scarcity.
Pledged as security for a loan.

n: Still others borrowed against their land to pay the Persian king’s taxes. Imperial taxes were heavy, and the poor were caught between taxes and lenders.

f.g: Taxes owed to the Persian king.

n: Their bitter cry: we are the same flesh and blood as the rich, yet our children are being sold into servitude to pay debts, and we can’t buy them back because others now own our land.

f.w: our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren
f.g: We are of the same family and people.
Buy back from servitude.

n: Nehemiah is angry — righteously so. Injustice toward the poor is a serious offense against God.
He first thinks it through, then confronts the leaders openly. Charging interest to fellow Israelites in need was forbidden by the law of Moses.

f.g: I thought it over carefully.
Charging interest on loans; here also taking pledges from the poor.

n: Nehemiah points out the irony: we have spent money buying back Jews sold to foreigners, and now you are selling your own brothers! The nobles have no answer.

f.g: Fell silent.

n: He appeals to their witness before the nations. Mistreating one another gives their enemies a reason to mock Israel and its God.

f.w: walk in the fear of our God
f.g: Live with reverent respect for God.

n: Nehemiah admits that he and his men also lent money and grain. He includes himself: “let us” stop this practice.

f.g: Stop, give up.

n: He calls for immediate restitution: give back the land, homes, and the interest charged. True repentance includes making things right.

f.g: Olive groves.
One percent — likely a monthly interest rate, about 12 percent a year.

n: The nobles agree. To make it binding, Nehemiah has them swear an oath before the priests.
Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his robe as a symbol: may God shake out anyone who breaks this promise. The people say “Amen,” praise the Lord, and keep their word.

f.g: Shook out the fold of his garment, which was used like a pocket — an acted-out curse.
Hebrew for “so be it” or “truly.”

n: Nehemiah now looks back over his twelve years as governor (445–433 BC). He never claimed the food allowance a governor was entitled to collect from the people.

f.g: The governor’s official food allowance, paid by taxes on the people.

n: Earlier governors had burdened the people with heavy charges, and their staff bullied the people. Nehemiah refused to, out of reverence for God.

f.g: Burdensome, demanding payment.
A shekel was a weight of silver, about 0.4 ounce (11 grams).

f.w: because of the fear of God

n: Rather than using his position to buy up land cheaply from struggling families, Nehemiah and his servants worked on the wall.

f.g: He did not profit from others’ hardship.

n: He fed 150 officials daily at his own table, plus visitors from other nations — paying from his own resources.

f.g: Governors were expected to host officials and guests.

n: His daily menu was large, yet he still didn’t demand the governor’s allowance, because the people were already weighed down. Leaders who serve without burdening others follow a higher pattern.

f.w: the bondage was heavy upon this people
store of all sorts of wine
f.g: An abundant supply of wine.

n: Nehemiah ends with a short prayer, one of several in his memoir: remember me for good. He looks to God, not to people, for his reward.

f.w: Think upon me, my God, for good
